newsitem.title: USA: Texas Instruments posts $148 million loss.
newsitem.headline: Texas Instruments posts $148 million loss.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc., battered by plunging prices for computer memory chips, said Tuesday it lost $148 million in the third quarter and would offer early retirement to 5,300 employees to cut costs.

The Dallas-based semiconductor giant said the loss, equal to 78 cents a share, was due to a one-time charge of $192 million for research and development costs associated with its acquisition this year of Silicon Systems Inc.

Still, even excluding the charge, TI's third-quarter net income plunged to $44 million, or 23 cents a share, from $289 million, or $1.48 a share, a year ago, before the prices of computer chips began to deteriorate drastically.
The earnings, equal to 23 cents a share, however, were better than Wall Street estimates of 20 cents a share, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' estimates.
The company said revenues declined to $2.84 billion from $3.43 billion in the third quarter of 1995.
TI said the earnings slump was due to sharply lower prices for memory chips, long its core product.

"We are not satisfied with our performance over the last two quarters," Chief Executive Thomas Engibous said in a statement. "We are accelerating our pace to compete and win in high-growth markets, add stability to our business and create higher value-added solutions for our customers."
He said that in addition to the early retirement programme, the company would also significantly reduce its capital spending next year.
The company said the voluntary retirement programme would be offered in most of its U.S. business and support areas.

"In view of the current market environment and the need to keep costs in line with demand, TI is offering an enhanced early retirement programme to about 5,300 eligible U.S.-based employees. Participation in the programme is voluntary," the company said.

It also said it would "significantly" reduce capital spending in 1997, following the completion of high-level investment this year to build the base for advanced logic and mixed-signal manufacturing and new R&D facilities in Dallas.

Texas Instruments said prices for dynamic random access memory chips, or DRAMs, have turned higher in recent weeks after a dramatic drop since late last year, but the market "is likely to remain volatile for the near-term."
TI said the improvement was due to inventory depletion and customers' anticipation of seasonally stronger personal computer sales.
It added that it expected the world semiconductor market to decline by about 10 percent this year but show a "moderate" recovery in 1997.

TI said the combination of higher fixed investment and the dramatic drop in DRAM prices -- down 80 percent from the 1995 third quarter -- meant its memory operations ran a loss in the third quarter but the overall semiconductor business was profitable.
TI's stock closed at $55.625 Monday on the New York Stock Exchange.
